intro.title: For Roma in Moldova, building a future means navigating compounding disadvantages in an uncertain present
intro.content:
Roma face disadvantages across education, work, housing, health and public services — with discrimination cutting through all of them. These pressures compound: exclusion in one area narrows what is possible in the next, so barriers accumulate within households and shape opportunities for the next generation.

Shared barriers affect people differently depending on the circumstance. Gender, age or place pull households onto different paths. Women are less likely to enter paid work, while men’s greater access often leads to informal jobs with little protection. For children, frequent moves can interrupt schooling; for older people, securing treatment and care becomes a greater concern. Where families live shapes these paths too: home ownership can offer little security amid worn-out infrastructure and arrears, and nearby services can remain out of reach because of discrimination.

Despite this, Roma families continue to pursue better lives. They assemble strategies from seasonal, informal or entrepreneurial work, undertake care and housing labour for each other, and strive for their children to stay at school. They are resilient, managing what the day demands while aspiring for better and secure lives.

text.title: Same localities, different realities
text.content:
Roma and non-Roma people live side by side in the same localities. Yet their experiences can be very different.

To better understand these disparities, Roma households were surveyed along with their non-Roma neighbours.
text.methodology: This story is based on 2025 Multi-Country Survey on Socio-Economic Vulnerabilities of Roma, covering 700 Roma and 300 non-Roma households across 63 localities, micro-narratives study collecting 547 personal accounts of Roma individuals and geospatial analysis of access to services.

text.title: Disadvantages that carry through life
text.content:
These disadvantages begin in <Badge>education</Badge>, put <Badge>economic security</Badge> at risk, and shape everyday life through <Badge>living conditions</Badge> and <Badge>health</Badge>, while <Badge>discrimination</Badge> cuts across all these areas.

To make these differences easier to see and compare across areas, each result is shown out of 100 people.

vizContent.title: Have not completed secondary education
vizContent.subTitle: Adults aged 18 to 65. Only 11 in 100 Roma have completed secondary education, against 60 in 100 non-Roma.

text.title: Education gaps extend into adult life
text.content: The discrepancy in formal schooling leaves Roma at a disadvantage when seeking work, pursuing further learning or accessing services.

text.title: Finding work does not ensure a secure livelihood
text.content: Informal work often leaves Roma with uncertain earnings and little social protection, making it harder to cover household costs and plan ahead.

vizContent.title: Live in overcrowded homes
vizContent.subTitle: Too few rooms for the household

text.title: Having a roof does not ensure adequate space, sanitation or warmth
text.content: Many Roma families live in overcrowded houses with damp and insufficient indoor sanitation. Insecure renting conditions can force families to move frequently.

text.title: Poor health constrains opportunities for many Roma during their working years
text.content: Roma adults report poor health more often, and many lack insurance. Caring for relatives often means giving up paid work.

vizContent.title: Experienced discrimination in the past year
vizContent.subTitle: Because of ethnicity, skin colour or language.

text.title: Unequal treatment and administrative barriers restrict access to opportunities and support
text.content: A third of Roma faced discrimination in the past year. Services are nearby, but paperwork and repeated visits keep them out of reach.
